prompt:
# Write one behaviour-tree node that ADJUSTS an existing navigator

You are writing a single node for the behaviour tree of a Unitree Go2 quadruped
navigating an indoor space it has no map of.

Below the node is an inherited, pretrained, **frozen** locomotion policy. The
only thing anything ever sends the robot is a Twist — `(vx, vy, wz)`. You never
touch the policy, the gait, or the joints.

**You are not writing the navigator.** A navigator already exists, it already
drives, and it will keep driving whether or not your node does anything. Your
node sits above it and revises what it asked for.

Return **one Python module**, in one fenced ```python block, and nothing else
that looks like code. Everything you want to say in prose, say outside the
fence. What the module must contain is set out in "What to return" at the end.

## How the tree runs: a layered command pipeline

Every node in the tree ticks, **every step, in order**. Nothing short-circuits
anything.

    Layer[ ports, BASE, node_1, node_2, ... ]
             ^      ^      ^
             |      |      `- each may revise the fields it declared
             |      `-------- proposes a whole command, every tick
             `--------------- publishes a few facts from the sensors

The **base** is a general indoor navigator. It gets the robot most of the way
most of the time, it handles the awkward cases, and it never declines to act.
Each later node may then adjust individual fields of what the base proposed.

This is subsumption: a competent low layer, refined by narrow higher ones. Your
node is one of the higher ones.

**So the thing you are writing is small.** It does one thing to one part of the
command, under one condition, and the rest of the time it stays out of the way.

## The one hard rule: you declare which fields you may write

Your class declares `WRITES` — the Twist fields it is allowed to touch:

```python
WRITES = ("vx",)            # may bound or set forward speed, nothing else
WRITES = ("wz",)            # may steer, but may not change speed
WRITES = ("vx", "wz")       # both. Only if the mechanism genuinely needs both.
```

This is **enforced, not advisory.** Writing a field you did not declare raises
immediately and the node is rejected. Declare the smallest set your mechanism
actually needs — a node that declares all three is claiming to be a navigator,
and it will be judged as one.

Two ways to write, and they are the only two:

```python
ports.cap(vx=0.35)       # min(|pending|, 0.35), sign kept. Never speeds up.
ports.adjust(wz=0.8)     # replaces the field outright. Last writer wins.
```

Prefer `cap` whenever the mechanism is a limit, a bound, or a "no faster than"
— it composes with other caps in any order, which `adjust` does not.

And you can see what the base asked for:

```python
pending = ports.command          # a Command(vx, vy, wz). Never None when you
                                 # tick, because the base ticks before you.
if pending.vx > my_limit:
    ports.cap(vx=my_limit)
```

**Do not call `ports.drive(...)`.** That writes the whole command and is the
base's job; it raises for a node that narrowed `WRITES`.

## Declining is a first-class outcome, and it is free

Return `Status.FAILURE` from `precondition`, or simply write nothing in `tick`,
and the base's command passes through **byte-identical**. The robot behaves
exactly as if your node were not in the tree.

That matters more than it sounds. Your node's contribution is measured by adding
it to the tree and re-running the same worlds: it can only be credited for the
episodes it changes, and it is blamed for every episode it breaks. A node that
acts only when its trigger genuinely holds is a good node. A node that fires on
every tick has replaced the base rather than supported it, and it will be
measured as having done so.

## The node contract

A leaf is one of three kinds, and the kind is the class you subclass:

- **`Condition`** — answers one question about the world and publishes it as a
  port. Never touches the Twist.
- **`Action`** — the only kind that may touch the Twist. With a narrowed
  `WRITES` it is a *modifier*, which is what you are writing.
- **`Decorator`** — wraps exactly one child and governs whether the child runs.
  Never touches the Twist itself.

Your class declares, as class attributes:

| Attribute | What it is |
|---|---|
| `WRITES` | the Twist fields this node may write. See above. |
| `PORTS` | a tuple of `Port` — the typed interface between nodes. See below. |
| `PRECONDITION` | one sentence: when this node applies |
| `EFFECT` | one sentence: what this node changes |
| `TAGS` | a tuple of short strings, for retrieval |

and implements:

```python
def reset(self, scenario, rng):    # clear per-episode state. optional.
def precondition(self, obs, ports) -> bool:   # default: always True
def tick(self, obs, ports) -> Status:         # Status.SUCCESS / FAILURE / RUNNING
```

**One precondition and one effect.** A node that needs two of either is two
nodes. This is not a style rule: contribution is measured by adding one node at
a time, and a node with two effects is attributable to neither.

**No coupling to a specific scenario.** Your node will be run on procedurally
generated worlds you have never seen. It may not name a room, a coordinate, a
doorway or a map. Anything it knows about the world it learns through `obs` at
tick time.

### Ports

Ports are how nodes pass information to each other. They are **not** a
blackboard: at tick time you are handed a `PortView` restricted to exactly the
ports you declared, and touching anything else raises immediately.

```python
Port(name, PortType.X, Direction.IN)    # you read it:   value = ports["name"]
Port(name, PortType.X, Direction.OUT)   # you write it:  ports["name"] = value
```

The port vocabulary is **closed**. These seven types and no others:

| `PortType` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `POSE` | `(x, y, yaw)` — a belief about where the robot is, never ground truth |
| `BEARING` | radians, robot frame unless the port name says otherwise |
| `SPEED` | m/s, non-negative |
| `RANGES` | an array of beam returns, metres |
| `CONFIDENCE` | `[0, 1]` — how much to trust something |
| `FLAG` | a boolean fact about the episode |
| `REGION` | an area of the floor, `(x, y, radius)` |

Three ports are always published before your node ticks, so you may declare any
of them as inputs: `goal_known` (FLAG), `pose` (POSE), `ranges` (RANGES).
Anything else you declare as an input must be published by another node earlier
in the Layer, and if nothing does, the tree refuses to build.

Publish an OUT port when the quantity you computed is genuinely useful to
someone else — a limit, a bearing, a confidence. Do not publish your own
internal state.

### What to import

Exactly these, and nothing else.

```python
import math
import numpy as np

from core.observation import Command
from nodes.contract import (Action, Condition, Decorator, Direction, Port,
                            PortType, Status)
```

Import only what you use. You will usually not need `Command` at all: a modifier
revises fields, it does not construct commands.

### What your node can see

`tick` is handed an `Observation`, frozen, one per control step:

```python
obs.t                   # sim seconds since the episode started
obs.ranges              # np.ndarray, 181 beams, metres, inf where no return
obs.range_angles        # np.ndarray, beam bearings in the ROBOT frame, radians
obs.range_max           # 6.0 — what "as far as I can see" means
obs.pose_estimate       # (x, y, yaw) — the BELIEF about our pose, not the truth
obs.pose_error_estimate # scalar, metres — how wrong we think the belief is
obs.contact             # bool — are we touching something right now
obs.goal                # (x, y), or None meaning NOT DISCLOSED
```

Two of these are traps and both are deliberate:

- **`pose_estimate` is a belief.** On some scenarios a seeded random walk is
  added to it and it drifts away from the truth. Ground truth is never in
  `Observation`; the runner keeps it for scoring only.
- **`obs.goal` may be `None`**, meaning the goal exists and the episode is still
  scored against it, but this robot has not found it yet. It **latches**: once
  disclosed it stays disclosed. Your node runs on scenarios that withhold the
  goal and on scenarios that do not, so **handle `None` explicitly**. Do not
  assume a tuple.

The scan is 181 beams over a full circle, so `obs.ranges[0]` is not the front —
find the beam you want through `obs.range_angles`.

Speeds are saturated by the runner to `|vx|, |vy| <= 0.8 m/s` and
`|wz| <= 1.0 rad/s`. Asking for more is not an error; it is just clipped.

## The task family this node has to be useful for

Reach a goal whose position is known, in an indoor space with no map. Walls and furniture occlude; the route is not a straight line and the obstruction is often not visible until the robot is close to it.

## What to base the node on

A principle card has been written for this task. **Implement this principle and
nothing else.**

```yaml
id: dynamic_window_velocity_search
node_name: SelectVelocityByDynamicWindow

mechanism: Collision avoidance is posed as a constrained search in VELOCITY space rather than in position space. At each control step the controller considers a two-dimensional set of candidate commands (forward speed v, turn rate omega), each of which implies a circular arc the robot would follow if that command were held. The set is cut down twice. First by REACHABILITY: only velocities attainable from the current velocity within one short acceleration-limited interval are considered, so the chosen command is one the body can actually produce next step rather than one it would have to teleport to. Second by ADMISSIBILITY: a candidate survives only if the robot, travelling that arc, could still brake to a standstill before reaching the nearest obstacle lying on it - formally v <= sqrt(2 * dist(v,omega) * a_brake), where dist is the free arc length. Among the survivors, one command is chosen by maximising a weighted sum of three normalised terms: alignment of the resulting heading with the target direction, clearance (the free arc length), and speed. It helps because safety becomes a hard feasibility constraint derived from physics - an inadmissible command is never even scored - while goal progress and speed remain soft preferences traded off against clearance. Unlike a reactive repulsion field, it never commands a velocity from which stopping is impossible, and unlike pure goal-seeking it prefers arcs with room to spare when several arcs make comparable progress.

trigger: Active whenever the tree must emit a Twist while moving toward a target direction AND the local surroundings are constrained enough that an unconstrained command could be unsafe: at least one lidar beam whose bearing satisfies |range_angles| <= pi/2 returns a finite range below 2.5 m. When every forward beam is beyond 2.5 m (or all are inf) the constraint set is the whole window and the node should yield to a cheaper straight-line pursuit leaf. Requires at least one finite lidar return; with a fully inf scan the precondition fails.

derivation: MOTION MODEL. Search only over (vx, wz) with vy = 0, because the arc model underlying the braking condition assumes motion along a circle of radius vx/wz; a nonzero vy would invalidate every dist() computation. Search bounds are the actuation saturations: vx in [0, 0.8] m/s (no reverse - the lidar is omnidirectional but the objective's heading term makes reverse arcs self-defeating) and wz in [-1.0, 1.0] rad/s. DYNAMIC WINDOW. The frozen locomotion policy hides the true acceleration limits, so they are estimated, and these numbers are MINE, not the paper's: a_v = 2.0 m/s^2 and a_w = 4.0 rad/s^2, being roughly the rate at which a ~15 kg quadruped can change commanded body velocity without the tracker falling behind. With a window horizon T_w = 0.25 s (about the settling time of the policy on a step command) the window is vx in [vx_prev - 0.5, vx_prev + 0.5] and wz in [wz_prev - 1.0, wz_prev + 1.0], intersected with the saturation box. vx_prev/wz_prev are the command this node emitted last step (initialise to 0,0). Sample it on a grid of 11 vx values by 21 wz values = 231 candidates; at ~2e2 candidates times ~181 beams this is a few 1e4 operations per step, cheap enough for a control-rate leaf. dist(v,omega). For each candidate, convert every finite lidar return to a point (r*cos(theta), r*sin(theta)) in the robot frame. Forward-simulate the arc for T_sim = 2.0 s (2.0 s * 0.8 m/s = 1.6 m, comfortably longer than the worst-case braking distance below) and take dist = arc length travelled until the swept disc of radius r_safe = 0.35 m first contains a lidar point, else dist = min(range_max, T_sim * |v|) = at most 6.0 m. r_safe = 0.35 m is the Go2's circumscribed body radius (~0.70 m long, ~0.31 m wide) with no extra margin, so the margin is bought by the clearance term, not smuggled in here. ADMISSIBILITY. Keep a candidate iff |v| <= sqrt(2 * dist * a_brake) with a_brake = 2.0 m/s^2 - the paper's condition, with the Go2 number substituted. At the top speed 0.8 m/s this demands dist >= 0.16 m of free arc. Apply the rotational analogue |wz| <= sqrt(2 * dist_ang * a_w) where dist_ang is the arc angle to first contact. If the admissible set is EMPTY, emit (0, 0, 0) and return FAILURE so a recovery leaf takes over; do not emit the least-bad inadmissible command. OBJECTIVE. Score survivors with G = alpha*heading + beta*clear + gamma*speed, each term min-max normalised to [0,1] across the surviving set (this is the role of the paper's smoothing/normalisation operator sigma). heading = 1 - |wrap_to_pi(bearing_to_target - yaw_after_T_w)| / pi, where the target bearing is computed from goal and pose_estimate when goal is not None, and otherwise defaults to the robot's current heading, which makes the node degrade gracefully into "hold the committed direction on the fastest safe arc". clear = min(dist, 2.0) / 2.0, saturating at 2.0 m because extra room beyond two metres should not outbid goal progress. speed = |v| / 0.8. Weights alpha = 0.6, beta = 0.3, gamma = 0.1 are MINE: heading dominates so the node still makes progress, clearance is half of heading's weight so it can flip the choice between two arcs of similar bearing, and speed only breaks ties. Emit the argmax as (vx, 0, wz). DRIFT ROBUSTNESS. Two of the three terms (clear, speed) and both constraints are computed purely in the robot frame from lidar, so pose drift and a large pose_error_estimate degrade only goal alignment, never the safety guarantee.

prediction:
  statement: On unmapped indoor navigation with occluding walls and furniture, replacing the baseline's command selection with the dynamic-window admissible-velocity search reduces the mean number of collisions per episode by at least 50% relative to goal_seeker, over a fixed set of seeds.
  metric: collisions
  baseline: goal_seeker
  min_effect: 0.5
  cost_metric: time_to_goal
```

The fields mean what they say, and each one has a job:

- **mechanism** — what happens, and why it helps. This is the node body.
- **trigger** — when it applies. This is the precondition, and under the layered
  pipeline it is doing real work: outside the trigger your node must leave the
  base's command alone.
- **derivation** — how the principle becomes a rule for a Go2 with a 181-beam 2D
  scan. Where the derivation and your instincts disagree, follow the derivation:
  it is what the card is for.
- **prediction** — the falsifiable claim. **Restate it verbatim** in
  `PREDICTION`: the metric, the baseline and the minimum effect are the card's,
  not yours.
- **node_name** — what the leaf is called. Use it as the class name.

You are not told where this principle came from, and you do not need to know.
A card is a card: extracted from a paper, recalled from one, or devised from
nothing, it is implemented the same way and judged by the same harness.

If you believe a different mechanism would score better, that belief is not what
is being measured here — a node that quietly implements something else makes the
card untestable.

**If the principle genuinely cannot be expressed as an adjustment to an existing
navigator, say so in prose and write the closest honest version you can.** Some
mechanisms are whole navigators and this pipeline cannot represent them; that is
a finding about the corpus, and it is more useful than a node that pretends.

## How this node will be judged

Two steps, both automatic, neither of which you can talk round.

1. **Validity.** Your module is loaded, wired into
   `Layer[ports, BASE, your node]`, and ticked over a rollout. It has to build,
   its ports have to be satisfiable, and it must not raise. Writing a Twist
   field you did not declare fails here.
2. **Contribution.** The tree above is run over a suite of randomly generated
   indoor worlds and compared, on identical worlds, against the base alone. What
   is reported is how many worlds your node **fixed** (the base failed, the pair
   succeeded) and how many it **broke** (the reverse).

You do not write the worlds and you have never seen them. There is no
micro-world to build and no baseline to name — that is deliberate, because a
generator that writes both the mechanism and the world that judges it is
grading its own homework.

## Rules the candidate is checked against

Your module is rejected, automatically, if any of these is false. The rejection
is recorded with its reason; it is not a catastrophe, but it is a wasted node.

- It parses, and it imports **only** from this list:
  `math`, `numpy`, `core.observation`, `nodes.contract`, `harness.micro`.
  Nothing else — no `os`, no file access, no `core.scenario`, no `core.geometry`.
  Your node learns about the world through `obs`, and that restriction is what
  makes "no coupling to a specific scenario" true rather than promised.
- It defines **exactly one** `Condition`, `Action` or `Decorator` subclass.
- Every port type is one of the seven. `EFFECT` and `PRECONDITION` are non-empty.
- `WRITES` names only `vx`, `vy` and `wz`, and the node writes nothing outside
  it.

## What to return

One fenced ```python block. It contains exactly two things:

1. **One node class** — normally an `Action` with a narrowed `WRITES`.
2. **`PREDICTION`** — a module-level dict, the card's falsifiable claim:

   ```python
   PREDICTION = {
       "metric": "goal_reached",     # what gets better
       "baseline": "base",           # what it gets better than
       "min_effect": 0.5,            # by at least how much
       "cost_metric": "time_to_goal" # what it makes WORSE. Required, and honest.
   }
   ```

   `cost_metric` may be `""` only if you genuinely believe the mechanism costs
   nothing, and you should be suspicious of that belief.

**No `micro()`.** Do not write one; it is not read.

Put a short docstring on the class saying what mechanism it implements, which
Twist field it revises and why, and when it declines. Write it as you would
write code someone else has to maintain: comments where a choice is not obvious,
and no comments restating the line below them.

response.text:
This card is, honestly, a whole navigator wearing a modifier's coat: DWA *selects* a command rather than revising one, so inside its trigger it fully overwrites `vx` and `wz` with `adjust`. I've kept it as narrow as the pipeline allows in two ways:

- **`WRITES = ("vx", "wz")`, not all three.** The derivation searches over `(vx, wz)` with `vy = 0`, so those are the only fields the mechanism produces. I deliberately did *not* declare `vy` just to zero it — that would buy a marginally more faithful arc model at the price of claiming the whole Twist. The cost is real and worth stating: if the base commands a lateral velocity, the circular-arc model behind `dist(v, ω)` is only approximate for that step, and the braking guarantee degrades accordingly.
- **The trigger does the restraint.** Outside clutter (no finite forward beam under 2.5 m) or with a fully-inf scan, `precondition` returns `False` and the base passes through byte-identical.

Two places where I had to make a call the card underdetermines:

1. **Stale window after declining.** The derivation says `vx_prev/wz_prev` is "the command this node emitted last step". If the node was *inactive* last step, the robot is actually executing the base's command, so a window centred on our stale emission would be a window around a velocity the body isn't at — which is exactly what the reachability constraint exists to prevent. I re-seed the window from `ports.command` on the first active tick after any gap, and track that with `_was_active`.
2. **Pure-rotation candidates.** `v = 0` gives zero free arc length, hence `clear = 0`, but it is always admissible (`0 <= sqrt(0)`) and the disc body sweeps no new area while spinning, so `dist_ang` is left free. That gives the search a legal turn-in-place escape instead of an empty admissible set. Note that when `vx_prev` is high the window floor is `vx_prev - 0.5 > 0`, so `v = 0` may not be sampled at all — in that case the set can still come back empty, and the card's instruction applies: emit zero and return `FAILURE` rather than the least-bad inadmissible command.

Arc distances are computed analytically (circle-to-circle containment about the arc centre, with a first-order `r_safe/|R|` angular slack that errs early, i.e. conservative), not by forward time-stepping — 231 candidates × ~181 beams, which keeps it in the few-1e4-ops budget the derivation asks for.

```python
import math

import numpy as np

from nodes.contract import Action, Direction, Port, PortType, Status


class SelectVelocityByDynamicWindow(Action):
    """Dynamic-window admissible-velocity search over (vx, wz).

    Poses collision avoidance as a constrained search in velocity space: sample
    the commands reachable from the current velocity within one acceleration-
    limited interval, discard every candidate from which the robot could not
    brake to a standstill before the first obstacle on the arc it implies, and
    pick the survivor maximising a weighted sum of goal alignment, clearance
    and speed.

    Revises `vx` and `wz` because those are exactly the two degrees of freedom
    the arc model searches over; it writes them with `adjust` rather than `cap`
    because the mechanism *selects* a velocity (which may be faster or turn the
    other way than the base asked) rather than bounding one. `vy` is left to the
    base -- zeroing it would make the arc model exact but would mean declaring
    the whole Twist.

    Declines (leaving the base's command untouched, byte-identical) when the
    surroundings are not constrained: no finite lidar return within 2.5 m at a
    bearing of |theta| <= pi/2, or a fully infinite scan. Returns FAILURE after
    emitting a stop when the admissible set is empty, so a recovery leaf can
    take over instead of this node guessing at a least-bad unsafe command.
    """

    WRITES = ("vx", "wz")
    PORTS = (Port("dwa_safe_speed", PortType.SPEED, Direction.OUT),)
    PRECONDITION = (
        "The robot is in locally constrained surroundings: at least one lidar "
        "beam with |bearing| <= pi/2 returns a finite range below 2.5 m."
    )
    EFFECT = (
        "Replaces the forward speed and turn rate with the highest-scoring "
        "velocity from which the robot can still brake before the nearest "
        "obstacle on the arc that velocity implies."
    )
    TAGS = ("dynamic_window", "velocity_space", "admissibility", "clearance",
            "local_avoidance", "lidar")

    # Actuation saturations (the runner clips to these anyway).
    V_MAX = 0.8
    W_MAX = 1.0

    # Estimated acceleration limits of the frozen locomotion policy: roughly
    # how fast a ~15 kg quadruped's tracker can follow a step in commanded body
    # velocity. These are the card's numbers, not measured ones.
    A_V = 2.0
    A_W = 4.0
    A_BRAKE = 2.0

    T_WINDOW = 0.25          # one window interval ~ policy settling time
    T_SIM = 2.0              # arc rollout horizon; 2.0 s * 0.8 m/s = 1.6 m
    R_SAFE = 0.35            # Go2 circumscribed body radius, no extra margin

    N_V = 11
    N_W = 21

    CLUTTER_RANGE = 2.5      # trigger threshold on forward beams
    CLEAR_SAT = 2.0          # clearance saturates here so room beyond 2 m
                             # cannot outbid goal progress

    ALPHA = 0.6              # heading
    BETA = 0.3               # clearance
    GAMMA = 0.1              # speed

    # Class-level defaults so the node is usable even if reset() is never called.
    _v_prev = 0.0
    _w_prev = 0.0
    _was_active = False

    def reset(self, scenario, rng):
        self._v_prev = 0.0
        self._w_prev = 0.0
        self._was_active = False

    def precondition(self, obs, ports) -> bool:
        ranges = np.asarray(obs.ranges, dtype=float)
        angles = np.asarray(obs.range_angles, dtype=float)
        finite = np.isfinite(ranges)
        if not finite.any():
            self._was_active = False
            return False

        forward = np.abs(angles) <= 0.5 * math.pi
        active = bool((finite & forward & (ranges < self.CLUTTER_RANGE)).any())
        if not active:
            # Remember that the base, not us, is driving: the next active tick
            # must build its reachable window around the base's velocity.
            self._was_active = False
        return active

    def tick(self, obs, ports) -> Status:
        pending = ports.command
        px, py = self._obstacle_points(obs)
        if px.size == 0:
            return Status.FAILURE

        if self._was_active:
            v_prev, w_prev = self._v_prev, self._w_prev
        else:
            # First active tick after a gap: the body is executing the base's
            # command, so that is the velocity we are actually reachable from.
            v_prev = float(np.clip(pending.vx, 0.0, self.V_MAX))
            w_prev = float(np.clip(pending.wz, -self.W_MAX, self.W_MAX))

        dv = self.A_V * self.T_WINDOW
        dw = self.A_W * self.T_WINDOW
        vs = np.linspace(max(0.0, v_prev - dv),
                         min(self.V_MAX, v_prev + dv), self.N_V)
        ws = np.linspace(max(-self.W_MAX, w_prev - dw),
                         min(self.W_MAX, w_prev + dw), self.N_W)
        V, W = np.meshgrid(vs, ws, indexing="ij")
        V = V.ravel()
        W = W.ravel()

        dist, dist_ang = self._arc_clearance(V, W, px, py, float(obs.range_max))

        # Hard feasibility: an inadmissible command is never scored.
        keep = ((V <= np.sqrt(2.0 * self.A_BRAKE * dist) + 1e-9)
                & (np.abs(W) <= np.sqrt(2.0 * self.A_W * dist_ang) + 1e-9))

        if not keep.any():
            ports.adjust(vx=0.0, wz=0.0)
            ports["dwa_safe_speed"] = 0.0
            self._v_prev = 0.0
            self._w_prev = 0.0
            self._was_active = True
            return Status.FAILURE

        Vk = V[keep]
        Wk = W[keep]
        dk = dist[keep]

        heading = 1.0 - np.abs(self._wrap(self._target_bearing(obs)
                                          - Wk * self.T_WINDOW)) / math.pi
        clear = np.minimum(dk, self.CLEAR_SAT) / self.CLEAR_SAT
        speed = np.abs(Vk) / self.V_MAX

        score = (self.ALPHA * self._normalise(heading)
                 + self.BETA * self._normalise(clear)
                 + self.GAMMA * self._normalise(speed))
        best = int(np.argmax(score))

        v_cmd = float(Vk[best])
        w_cmd = float(Wk[best])
        ports.adjust(vx=v_cmd, wz=w_cmd)
        ports["dwa_safe_speed"] = float(
            min(self.V_MAX, math.sqrt(2.0 * self.A_BRAKE * float(dk[best]))))

        self._v_prev = v_cmd
        self._w_prev = w_cmd
        self._was_active = True
        return Status.SUCCESS

    def _obstacle_points(self, obs):
        """Finite lidar returns as Cartesian points in the robot frame."""
        ranges = np.asarray(obs.ranges, dtype=float)
        angles = np.asarray(obs.range_angles, dtype=float)
        n = min(ranges.size, angles.size)
        ranges = ranges[:n]
        angles = angles[:n]
        good = np.isfinite(ranges) & (ranges > 1e-3)
        r = ranges[good]
        a = angles[good]
        return r * np.cos(a), r * np.sin(a)

    def _target_bearing(self, obs) -> float:
        """Bearing to the goal in the robot frame, or 0 if it is undisclosed.

        With no goal this degrades into "hold the committed heading on the
        fastest safe arc", which is the graceful fallback the card asks for.
        """
        goal = obs.goal
        if goal is None:
            return 0.0
        x, y, yaw = obs.pose_estimate
        return float(self._wrap(math.atan2(goal[1] - y, goal[0] - x) - yaw))

    def _arc_clearance(self, V, W, px, py, range_max):
        """Free arc length and free arc angle before the swept disc hits a point.

        Returned distances are capped at the rollout horizon and the sensor
        range, so an unobstructed arc scores the same as a very long one.
        """
        dist = np.minimum(range_max, self.T_SIM * V)
        dist_ang = np.minimum(math.pi, self.T_SIM * np.abs(W))

        straight = np.abs(W) < 1e-3
        curving = (~straight) & (V > 1e-6)

        if straight.any():
            # Swept disc travelling along +x: a point is struck when its
            # distance to the disc centre falls to R_SAFE.
            lateral = np.abs(py) <= self.R_SAFE
            if lateral.any():
                half = np.sqrt(np.maximum(self.R_SAFE ** 2 - py[lateral] ** 2, 0.0))
                s_enter = px[lateral] - half
                s_exit = px[lateral] + half
                ahead = s_exit >= 0.0
                if ahead.any():
                    d_line = float(np.maximum(s_enter[ahead], 0.0).min())
                    dist[straight] = np.minimum(dist[straight], d_line)

        if curving.any():
            Vc = V[curving]
            Wc = W[curving]
            R = Vc / Wc                      # signed turn radius
            aR = np.abs(R)
            sgn = np.sign(Wc)

            # Distance of each point from the arc centre (0, R); the swept disc
            # can only ever reach points within R_SAFE of the arc's own radius.
            rho = np.hypot(px[None, :], py[None, :] - R[:, None])
            hit = np.abs(rho - aR[:, None]) <= self.R_SAFE

            # Angle about the centre from the robot's start angle, measured in
            # the direction of travel; minus the angular slack corresponding to
            # the body radius, which makes contact register slightly early.
            beta = np.arctan2(py[None, :] - R[:, None], px[None, :])
            alpha0 = -0.5 * math.pi * sgn
            swept = np.mod((beta - alpha0[:, None]) * sgn[:, None], 2.0 * math.pi)
            slack = np.minimum(self.R_SAFE / aR, math.pi)
            swept = np.maximum(swept - slack[:, None], 0.0)

            first = np.where(hit, swept, np.inf).min(axis=1)
            dist[curving] = np.minimum(dist[curving], aR * first)
            dist_ang[curving] = np.minimum(dist_ang[curving], first)

        # Candidates with v == 0 keep dist == 0 (no arc) but an unconstrained
        # arc angle: spinning a disc body in place sweeps no new floor.
        return dist, dist_ang

    @staticmethod
    def _wrap(a):
        return np.arctan2(np.sin(a), np.cos(a))

    @staticmethod
    def _normalise(a):
        lo = float(a.min())
        hi = float(a.max())
        if hi - lo < 1e-9:
            return np.zeros_like(a)
        return (a - lo) / (hi - lo)
```

The cost metric is the card's and I believe it: the clearance term buys margin by taking wider arcs, the admissibility constraint caps speed near obstacles at `sqrt(2·dist·2.0)`, and the empty-set stop costs whole steps — all of which lengthen `time_to_goal` in exactly the cluttered episodes where the node is active.
